HomeBite

Final project report · Nicole Lin · MGT 409, AI Foundations for Managers, Yale SOM, Fall 2026

1. HomeBite

Adapt a dish from home to the ingredients you can actually buy at your store, with nutrition computed in code from USDA data.

AuthorNicole Lin
CourseMGT 409, AI Foundations for Managers, Yale SOM, Fall 2026
Codehttps://github.com/kl2278/homebite.git
AppNot hosted online. Runs locally from a fresh clone; setup measured at about 35 seconds in a fresh-clone test (see README). The README itself estimates about 5 minutes for a first-time user, because that includes creating the .env file.

HomeBite takes a dish that a student misses from home, for example Taiwanese beef noodle soup, together with the student's store and allergies. It breaks the dish into ingredients, finds substitutes for the ones that are hard to buy, but only from a product catalog for that store, writes the cooking steps, and compares the nutrition of the original and the adapted dish. Code, not the AI model, computes the nutrition numbers and checks allergens. It is a prototype: the catalog is a starter set of 163 illustrative items, not real store data.

At a glance
  • Design: five stages (Intake, Analyst, Substitution, Verifier, Writer) plus an input guard and output checks; the Verifier is pure code. Model: gpt-6-luna through Portkey.
  • Data: 3,000 USDA foods and 163 catalog items; 0 of the 163 catalog items have been verified against real store listings.
  • Cost and speed (20 live runs, 10 dishes x 2 configurations): baseline average $0.002414 per run and 33.2 seconds per run.
  • Checks: 188 automated tests pass without spending tokens; the safety demo passes 19/19 cases.
  • Honest result: a cheaper configuration cut cost by 16.9% but lowered the nutrition match rate from 91.7% to 82.0%, so I did not adopt it.

2. Motivation: who this is for

The problem

U.S. institutions hosted 1,177,766 international students in 2024/25, about 6% of total U.S. higher-education enrollment (Open Doors 2025). Many of them arrive in a food environment that is unfamiliar. A 2015 study with seven focus groups and 32 college-age international students at an urban U.S. university found that students described many dietary challenges when adapting to American culture, shaped by the food environment, the campus, religion and personal preferences. The authors also report dietary changes associated with undesirable health outcomes such as weight gain (Alakaam et al., 2015).

Where students shop matters. A master's thesis at East Carolina University (a survey of 142 international students in spring 2011, plus interviews) found that food choices were guided by whether students' native foods were available in local stores and by how long they had been in the U.S.; newcomers tended to look for familiar foods. Familiar food also carries meaning. In a small thesis study at one large public university (38 surveys and 11 interviews), 80% of the students who rated their sense of belonging differently for foods from their home country versus overall said they felt more belonging with those foods. A small qualitative sample, so a hint, not a measurement.

Money is part of the picture too. A survey of 853 students aged 18 to 34 at one Midwest university (April 2022) found food insecurity among 26.8% of international students, compared with 19.9% of White students and 35.6% of U.S.-born multicultural students; international students also used nutrition assistance programs, including the campus food pantry, more. One university only, so this shows the problem exists, not how large it is.

My own starting point

I am an international student from Taiwan. I love cooking and I'm passionate about nutrition. I find it challenging to get used to the food here in the US, and I miss my mom's cooking (or Taiwanese food in general) a lot. I designed this app because I think a lot of international students might share my experience and want to recreate some dishes from home.

How students cope today, and what it costs

The usual workarounds are a web search, asking a chatbot, asking family, or giving up on the dish. I timed one of them: searching Google for a vegetarian kimchi jjigae recipe took about 2 minutes. That is one dish, one attempt, timed by me. It produced a recipe only: I still had to look up the nutrition facts of any alternative ingredients myself, and the time does not include shopping or cooking. I did not measure what students spend in money or how often they give up, so I make no claim about either; the sources above support only that familiar food matters and that store availability shapes choices.

What HomeBite is not. It is not medical advice. It does not fix food insecurity. It is not a substitute for real store data: its catalog is a starter set of 163 illustrative items, and none of them has been checked against a real store listing.

Is this just another recipe or meal-planning app?

It is adjacent to that crowded category, and the difference is narrow. First, it starts from one specific dish from home and rebuilds it for the student's own store; it does not plan meals. Second, the model proposes and code disposes. Products can only come from the catalog. Nutrition is computed in code from USDA data, and ingredients without a USDA entry are listed as excluded. Allergen conflicts are checked by code and trigger a re-run of the substitution step. "No substitute, leave it out" is an allowed answer, and it happens often (sections 7 and 8). Third, safety and cost behavior is measured (20 live runs, and a safety demo that can be rerun).

Where it does not win

General chatbots are likely faster and cheap or free to use. Large retailers have real catalogs at scale. HomeBite's catalog is a 163-item starter set, so many dishes end with several ingredients left out. It is a prototype of a verification layer, not a finished product. I did not run a head-to-head test against a chatbot, so I make no claim about how one would handle the same dish.

4. The agents

HomeBite is a pipeline of small steps. Three are AI agents with a narrow job, one is plain code, and two more checks (an input guard and an output check) sit around them. Each AI agent returns a structured result; the Writer's fields are free text, and they are checked before they are shown.

StageJobToolsHands to the next stage
Input guardFree rules first (instruction overrides, requests for the prompt or keys, attempts to change store or allergies through the text), then one cheap classifier call. If the classifier cannot run, the request stops.Rules in code; one AI callPass, or a friendly message with no further tokens
IntakeTurns the text and sidebar settings into a request (dish, cuisine, servings, goals), or asks one clarifying question.NoneA structured request
AnalystBreaks the dish into ingredients with weights, flags those hard to find in a U.S. supermarket, and finds USDA entries.USDA searchIngredient list with USDA ids
SubstitutionFor each hard-to-find ingredient, picks a product that really comes back from a search of the student's store, or says there is none.Catalog search (store and allergies fixed by code), USDA searchA substitution plan
Verifier (pure code)Checks each substitute exists in the catalog, computes nutrition for both versions, runs the allergen check, lists unmatched ingredients. Re-runs Substitution once if there is a definite allergen conflict.Catalog lookup, nutrition math, allergen checkVerified ingredients, nutrition comparison, allergen result
WriterWrites the intro, the cooking steps and a note on what will taste different. It never sees nutrition numbers.NoneText
Output check (code)Rejects leaked prompts, key-like strings, invented numbers, nutrition claims and product names that were not confirmed. Retries once, then uses a plain template.Rules in codeThe text shown, or the template

Which model, and why

All AI calls use gpt-6-luna through Portkey with the course key. I chose the low-cost tier: $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.01 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens (course pricing slide), with cache writes at $0.125. The code calls the model through the Responses API, because the chat completions endpoint rejected function tools for this model (a comment in llm.py records this).

Why five stages instead of one prompt

Separation of duties. The model is good at reading a dish and proposing ingredients, and bad at being trusted with numbers, so numbers and checks are code. Each stage also gets its own small prompt and its own limits. I did not build or test a single-prompt version, so I cannot report how it would compare in cost or quality.

One real run, step by step

This is a live run of Kung pao chicken with Walmart selected and a peanut allergy. Settings go in the sidebar; the text box holds only the dish name.

Behind the page is a trace of every stage. The panels below are from the same run. The Intake panel shows the trusted settings and the student text in separate delimited blocks. The Analyst ran 21 nutrition searches (counted from the panel) in 3 requests. The Substitution agent searched the catalog five times and found a product for two of them. The Verifier, which is code, confirmed both products exist in the Walmart catalog, computed nutrition twice (original and adapted) and found one allergen conflict, which sent the run back to Substitution once.

Cross-check against the usage panel. The panels for Intake (311 in, 79 out), Analyst (8,116 in of which 2,855 cached, 1,769 out), Substitution (1,905 in, 711 out) and Writer (853 in, 422 out) add up to 11,185 input and 2,981 output tokens. The usage panel reports 13,661 input, 2,855 cached and 3,879 output tokens over 10 requests, so 2,476 input and 898 output tokens are not in the panels shown. That remainder is consistent with the guard call and the substitution re-run, whose panels are not in these screenshots. The cached tokens match exactly because only the Analyst had cache hits.

Design choices that are actually in the code

  • Trusted settings. Store, allergies, diet, servings and goal come from the sidebar and travel as configuration. The student's text is wrapped in delimiters and treated as data.
  • The Analyst is not told the student's allergies. It describes the traditional dish, so a conflicting ingredient reaches the code check instead of being silently dropped by the model.
  • Tool wrappers fix the store and allergies. The catalog search takes the store and allergy list from the run settings, not from the model's arguments, so text like a request to search another store cannot change them (tested).
  • A missing substitute is an allowed answer. If the model names a product that is not in the store's catalog, the Verifier downgrades it to no substitute.

5. Tokenomics

All numbers in this section come from 20 live runs: 10 dishes, each run once with the baseline configuration and once with a cost-saver configuration (section below). Costs are computed from token counts with the course prices; the guard stage is included in every total. Latency is wall-clock time. No run was flagged as a possible gateway cache hit.

The guard stage costs $0.000052 per request on average (337 input and 38 output tokens), which is 2.2% of the total. In the safety demo, two real classifier calls used 403 and 401 tokens. Output tokens carry most of the cost: they are priced at five times normal input, and output is 58.6% of baseline cost.

They exclude hosting, storage and bandwidth, and they do not model provider rate limits at 100 or 10,000 users. They are estimates from tokens and the course price slide, not an invoice. The per-day token cap of 3,000,000 tokens (input plus output) implies at most about $0.50 per day at the measured token mix, or $1.50 per day in the worst case where every capped token is an output token. The whole 20-run measurement used 242,278 input plus output tokens, about $0.044 at these prices.

Can the cost be cut?

I tested three levers, switchable by a settings object and off by default: put each agent's static instructions first and the dynamic text last (so provider prompt caching could apply), trim the Analyst and Writer prompts while keeping every safety rule, and add a batched nutrition lookup so the Analyst searches all ingredients in one call. The cost-saver configuration turns on all three together. Each dish was run once per configuration, alternating which went first.

Cost split per run: baseline $0.000967 fresh input, $0.000033 cached input, $0.001414 output; cost-saver $0.000728, $0.000006 and $0.001272. Tool calls fell by 75.3% and cost fell by 16.9%; the cost-saver was cheaper on 9 of 10 dishes. The combined cost-saver did not raise caching: cached input fell by 81.0%, so the savings came from fewer tokens, not from more cache hits. Because the three levers were tested together, I cannot say whether prompt order alone had any effect.

The cost-saver was not adopted. It cut cost, but the nutrition match rate fell from 91.7% to 82.0%, and it was lower on 7 of 10 dishes (equal on 3, higher on none), so this is unlikely to be noise alone. A lower match rate means more ingredients are left out of the nutrition totals. I tested the three levers together, so I cannot say which one caused the drop. With one run per dish, the sample is small. The app still runs the baseline configuration.

Defenses working

The classifier calls for the two declined requests used 342 input and 41 output tokens (medical) and 341 input and 67 output tokens (extreme restriction), one request each, as the usage tables show. The safety demo (19/19 cases) covers the injection, key-leak, prompt-leak, store and allergy overrides, oversized input, forced tool loop, tool-call flood, session cap, rate limit, an invented number and product, and the kung pao peanut case.

Two live allergen runs

Peanut allergy, Kung pao chicken, Walmart. The first check flagged peanuts as a definite conflict and the substitution step was re-run once. Peanuts were left out of the recipe and struck through on the page; three other ingredients with no store match (dried red chilies, Chinese black vinegar and Shaoxing wine) were left out too, so four items were left out in total. The page shows a yellow warning, not a green box, because soy sauce, cornstarch and vegetable oil could not be confirmed peanut-free from the catalog or keyword list.

Fish allergy, Vietnamese chicken pho, Aldi (a fresh-clone check; the figures come from my Prompt 9 report, not from the repo logs): 44 seconds, 16,373 input tokens (4,328 cached, 5,406 cache-write), 3,794 output tokens, 11 requests, about $0.0033. The first pass flagged fish sauce and the substitution re-run removed it.

A problem the measurement found, and the fix

In the 20-run measurement, a gluten-allergy dish (Japanese chicken katsu curry) kept panko in the final recipe in both configurations, because the allergen keyword list had no entry for panko; it was only marked uncertain. I extended the keyword list (whole-word matching, so nutmeg and eggplant are not flagged). A before-and-after check on all saved results (logs/allergen_fix_check.md) shows only that dish changed: 2 of 14 saved results with an allergy (the two katsu curry runs). A new live run of the dish flagged panko, flour and soy sauce, re-ran the substitution step, and removed all three, so panko is no longer in the final recipe. A later check of noodle types (Prompt 8, with tests) found that rice vermicelli had been treated as safe for gluten rather than uncertain. That is fixed: rice, glass and sweet-potato noodles are now uncertain; wheat noodles, ramen, udon and soba stay definite conflicts.

What is not proven

  • The role-play jailbreak case in the demo was stopped by the AI provider's own content filter before my classifier answered, so it does not show my classifier working.
  • The red not-safe screen for a remaining allergen conflict was tested offline with a fake model only. In the live runs, the re-run always removed the conflict.
  • The allergen check uses catalog tags and a keyword list. It is not a guarantee. Ingredients such as Worcestershire sauce stay uncertain, and the page asks the student to check the label.
  • Allergen behavior was observed on 7 dishes in the measurement (14 runs) plus the demo and the live runs shown here, never with a real catalog.

7. Impact

Measured results are marked as measured; everything else is potential.

(a) One real user test

A friend, Alex, tried HomeBite in person on my laptop and agreed to be named by first name. He entered his mom's potato beef stew with Whole Foods selected, no allergies, the lower-sodium goal and 2 servings. The run took 18 seconds, used 5,458 input tokens (0 cached) and 1,776 output tokens over 5 requests, and cost an estimated $0.0015. No substitutions were needed (0 substitutes, 0 items left out). This was a single tester and a dish with no substitutions, so it tested usability, not the substitution engine.

He thought it was a cool concept, found the instructions easy to follow and the ingredient list clear. In his words: “This is fun to use and I look forward to recreating my mom's dishes using this!” His three ideas: allow multiple selections for allergens, dietary preferences and goals (for example low sodium and low calorie together; the allergy box already allows several choices, so he may not have noticed); show pictures of the dishes; and turn the input into a chatbot that talks with you about the dish.

(b) Time

My manual web search for one vegetarian kimchi jjigae recipe took about 2 minutes and gave a recipe only. HomeBite's measured run times were 16.1 to 56.6 seconds across the 20 runs, averaging 33.2 seconds for the baseline, and it returns an adapted ingredient list, steps, substitutes and a nutrition comparison. These are not like-for-like: one self-timed search for one dish against 20 runs of an app, and the search time excludes looking up nutrition.

(c) Cost

Measured: $0.002414 per run on average ($0.003646 at p90). Projected at 12 runs per user per month (my assumption): $0.03 per user per month.

(e) Reach

For context only, not a forecast: 1,177,766 international students were enrolled at U.S. institutions in 2024/25. I have no data on how many would use an app like this.

Measured: token use, cost and latency of 20 runs; safety demo results; one user test. Potential, not measured: time saved for students, savings in money, adoption, and any health benefit.

8. Limits and next steps

What does not work yet

  • The catalog is a starter set of 163 illustrative items, none verified against real listings. Over the 10 baseline runs, 7 ingredients got a substitute and 18 were left out.
  • Some ingredients have no USDA entry and are excluded from the nutrition totals; the page says which.
  • The Goal selector (for example lower sodium) is passed to the AI as context but is not enforced or verified by code, and the results page does not say whether the goal was met. Allergies and store are enforced by code; goals are not.
  • Nutrition differences between the original and the adapted dish mostly reflect ingredients that were left out or have no USDA entry, not a healthier recipe. Figure 19 shows this: sodium rises, which is consistent with the original dish's dark soy sauce having no USDA entry (so it is excluded) while its substitute does.
  • Allergies accept several selections; dietary preference and goal accept one choice each.
  • There are no dish pictures and no chat. The combined cost-saver did not raise caching. Most of the roughly 33 seconds is model generation, and I did not break latency down by stage.
  • Allergen checks are not a guarantee, and this is not medical advice. The Windows setup steps in the README are untested. Only one person tested the app.

If I had another month

  • Use real, licensed store data and verify it, replacing the starter catalog.
  • Have the Verifier compute whether a goal was met and show it on the page.
  • Allow several goals and diets at once.
  • Add conversational follow-ups, which would raise both cost and the safety surface.
  • Add dish images, after checking licensing.
  • Run a wider user study, with people who need substitutions.
  • Test the batched-lookup lever on its own, to find which lever lowered the nutrition match rate.
  • Add gluten-free and other allergen-safe items to the catalog, so the re-run has safe options to choose from.
